summary.text: The word used in the statement is only the tenth substitution iterate, extended by 1’s, so it has at most its finite length \(L\) many zeros and the out-of-range enumeration consequently gives \(a(n)=1\) for every \(n>L\). Taking \(N=L+2\), the estimate \(r>3/2\) yields \(|Nr-a(N)|=|Nr-1|>2\), contradicting the asserted bound.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\sigma\) be the substitution
\[
\sigma(0)=01,\qquad \sigma(1)=0100,
\]
and define finite words
\[
L_0=0,\qquad L_{j+1}=\sigma(L_j),
\]
where substitution is applied to every letter and the resulting words are concatenated.

The sequence used in the accepted disproof is defined from only the tenth such word. Put
\[
L=L_{10},\qquad \ell=|L|,
\]
and define a word-value function \(W\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) by
\[
W(k)=
\begin{cases}
\text{the letter of }L\text{ at zero-based position }k,&k<\ell,\\
1,&k\ge \ell.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus this definition agrees with the morphic word on the finite prefix \(L_{10}\), but every position after that prefix is assigned the default value \(1\).

Let
\[
Z=\{k\in\mathbb N:W(k)=0\}.
\]
Enumerate \(Z\) in increasing order, using zero-based enumeration. The enumeration convention in the statement is that if the requested element does not exist because the set is finite, its value is \(0\). Write this enumeration as \(e(m)\). The sequence in the accepted statement is then
\[
a(n)=e(n-1)+1.
\]
The subtraction here is subtraction in \(\mathbb N\); for the positive index used below it is ordinary subtraction. The added \(1\) converts a zero-based position into a one-based position.

We first show why this definition necessarily produces a spurious late value of \(a\). If \(k\ge\ell\), then by definition \(W(k)=1\), so such a \(k\) cannot belong to \(Z\). Consequently
\[
Z\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,\ell-1\}.
\]
In particular, \(Z\) is finite and has at most \(\ell\) elements.

Now choose
\[
N=\ell+2.
\]
Then \(N>0\), and the zero-based enumeration index used in \(a(N)\) is
\[
N-1=\ell+1.
\]
A set with at most \(\ell\) elements has no element with zero-based index \(\ell+1\). Therefore the default value in the enumeration applies:
\[
e(N-1)=0.
\]
It follows that
\[
a(N)=e(N-1)+1=1.
\]

For completeness, the counterexample index can be made explicit. If \(z_j\) and \(o_j\) denote the numbers of zeros and ones in \(L_j\), then each substituted zero contributes one zero and one one, while each substituted one contributes three zeros and one one. Hence
\[
z_{j+1}=z_j+3o_j,
\qquad
o_{j+1}=z_j+o_j,
\]
with \((z_0,o_0)=(1,0)\). Iterating gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r|r}
j&z_j&o_j&|L_j|\\ \hline
0&1&0&1\\
1&1&1&2\\
2&4&2&6\\
3&10&6&16\\
4&28&16&44\\
5&76&44&120\\
6&208&120&328\\
7&568&328&896\\
8&1552&896&2448\\
9&4240&2448&6688\\
10&11584&6688&18272.
\end{array}
\]
Thus \(\ell=18272\), and the chosen index is
\[
N=18274.
\]
Indeed, in this case there are exactly \(11584\) zeros available for enumeration, whereas \(a(N)\) asks for the zero with zero-based enumeration index \(18273\). No such zero exists under the truncated definition, so again \(a(18274)=1\).

It remains to compare this value with the conjectured estimate. Let
\[
r=\frac{3+\sqrt3}{3}.
\]
Since
\[
\left(\frac32\right)^2=\frac94<3
\]
and both \(3/2\) and \(\sqrt3\) are nonnegative, we have
\[
\frac32<\sqrt3.
\]
Therefore
\[
r=\frac{3+\sqrt3}{3}
  >\frac{3+3/2}{3}
  =\frac32.
\]
In particular, \(r>0\). Since \(N=\ell+2\ge2\), multiplication by the positive number \(r\) gives
\[
Nr\ge 2r>2\cdot\frac32=3.
\]
Using \(a(N)=1\), we conclude
\[
Nr-a(N)=Nr-1>2.
\]
Thus at the positive integer \(N\) (explicitly, \(N=18274\)) the asserted upper inequality
\[
Nr-a(N)<2
\]
fails. Equivalently,
\[
\left|Nr-a(N)\right|>2,
\]
so it cannot be less than \(2\). This disproves the universally quantified inequality for the sequence as it is defined in the accepted statement.

There is an important mathematical qualification. The canonical OEIS sequence is defined using the genuinely infinite fixed point of \(0\mapsto01\), \(1\mapsto0100\). The argument above instead uses a function that reads \(L_{10}\) and then declares every later letter to be \(1\); its zero set is therefore finite, and its out-of-range enumeration convention eventually makes \(a(n)=1\). Hence this accepted disproof exploits the truncation in the supplied definition. It does not, by itself, give a counterexample for the actual infinite fixed-point sequence A284852.
